```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r}
library(ipodr)
```

This vignette walks through a typical workflow on simulated quotes, where the
true risk-neutral distribution is known. All quantities refer to
\(Y = S_T/F\), the share price at expiry relative to the forward.

## 1. Quotes and chain preparation

The input is a long data frame with one row per quote for one underlying,
one observation date and one expiry: `strike`, `type` (call or put), `bid`,
`ask`, `rate` and either `ttm` (days) or `date` and `expiry`; optionally `oi`
(open interest) and `spot`. `sim_quotes()` produces such a data frame from a
distribution with an atom of mass `pod` at zero and a lognormal remainder.

```{r}
q <- sim_quotes(ttm = 182, sigma = 0.45, pod = 0.01)
head(q)
truth <- attr(q, "tail")
truth(c(0, 0.5, 0.8))
```

With quotes for several expiries, `select_expiry()` keeps the one closest to
182 days. `ipod_chain()` computes the put-call parity forward, keeps
out-of-the-money calls and puts (puts are converted to calls by parity) and
normalises strikes and prices by the forward.

```{r}
ch <- ipod_chain(q)
c(F = ch$F, T = ch$T, kmin = ch$kmin, kmax = ch$kmax, n = nrow(ch$quotes), ok = ch$ok)
```

`kmin` is the lowest quoted strike relative to the forward. Below it, the
quotes carry almost no information about the shape of the distribution.

## 2. A regularised point estimate

`ipod_fit()` fits a penalised maximum-entropy distribution: uniform on
\([0, d]\) (the barrier region) and exponentially tilted above, with price
tolerances from the bid-ask spread.

```{r}
fit <- ipod_fit(ch, d = 0.1, n_grid = 1000)
rbind(estimate = tail_prob(fit, c(0.5, 0.8)), truth = truth(c(0.5, 0.8)))
rnd_summary(fit)[c("pod", "p_eq80", "p_eq50", "q05", "kmin")]
```

The tail probability at 80% of the forward lies inside the quoted strike
range and is recovered closely. The PoD, the mass below the barrier, is not.

## 3. The PoD depends on an unidentified barrier

`ipod_profile()` refits over a grid of barriers. Every fit prices the quotes
within tolerance (`fit_in` is the share of quotes fitted within their
tolerance) and the tail probability at 80% barely moves, yet the PoD is
whatever the barrier makes it.

```{r}
pr <- ipod_profile(ch, d_grid = exp(seq(log(0.005), log(0.6), length.out = 12)), n_grid = 1000)
pr[, c("d", "pod", "fit_in", "p_eq80")]
range(pr$pod) / truth(0)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "PoD against the barrier on log scales"}
plot(pr$d, pr$pod, log = "xy", type = "b", xlab = "barrier d", ylab = "PoD",
     main = "Same quotes, different barriers")
abline(h = truth(0), lty = 2)
```

Barrier-selection rules pick one point of this profile by assumption:

```{r}
rbind(pod_select(pr, "mean"), pod_select(pr, "median"),
      pod_select(pr, "absolute"), pod_select(pr, "fixed", d = 0.1))
```

The `"absolute"` rule (barriers of 1 to 20 currency units) depends on the
nominal share price; a stock split changes it. In this example the true
distribution has an atom at zero, and every rule lands below it; for a
distribution without an atom, every rule would report a positive PoD. The
quotes cannot tell the two cases apart.

## 4. What the quotes identify

`tail_bounds()` gives the sharp lower and upper bounds of \(Q(Y \le a)\) over
all distributions consistent with the bid and ask quotes (Dillschneider 2026).
At `a = 0` the lower bound is zero whenever `kmin > 0`: the probability of
zero equity is never identified by option quotes alone.

```{r}
tb <- tail_bounds(ch, c(0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1))
tb$truth <- truth(tb$a)
tb
atm_iv_bounds(ch)
```

Report these bounds alongside any PoD or tail probability. The same bounds
for general payoffs are available by linear programming:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("lpSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
lp_bounds(ch, function(y) as.numeric(y <= 0.8))
```

## 5. Benchmarks

The at-the-money implied volatility, the lognormal tail at that volatility,
the drawdown and a distance to threshold are the natural benchmarks. The
anchored distress probability `adp()` is \(Q(S_T < \theta M)\) with \(M\) the
running peak of the share price; with `fit` it uses the fitted distribution,
with `sigma` the lognormal.

```{r}
iv <- atm_iv(ch)
iv
lognormal_tail(c(0.5, 0.8), sigma = iv, T = ch$T)
peak <- 1.6 * ch$F          # the share price has fallen 37.5% from its peak
c(rnd = adp(peak = peak, forward = ch$F, fit = fit),
  lognormal = adp(peak = peak, forward = ch$F, sigma = iv, T = ch$T))
```

## 6. Evaluating indicators across banks

The evaluation tools work on a panel with one row per bank and date. The
example below simulates eight banks observed weekly; three have an event at
the end of the sample and a volatility that drifts up towards it, with noise.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
dates <- as.Date("2023-01-04") + 7 * (0:19)
banks <- data.frame(bank = LETTERS[1:8],
                    event = as.Date(c(rep("2023-05-31", 3), rep(NA, 5))))
panel <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(banks)), function(i) {
  ev <- !is.na(banks$event[i])
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(dates), function(j) {
    sig <- if (ev) 0.30 + 0.02 * j + rnorm(1, 0, 0.08) else runif(1, 0.25, 0.6)
    chj <- ipod_chain(sim_quotes(sigma = max(sig, 0.1)))
    b0 <- tail_bounds(chj, 0.8)
    data.frame(bank = banks$bank[i], date = dates[j], event = banks$event[i],
               iv = atm_iv(chj), lo80 = b0$lower, hi80 = b0$upper)
  }))
}))
lab <- label_events(panel, horizon = 60)
table(lab$pos)
```

`auc_test()` reports pooled and bank-level AUCs and resamples event and
control banks as clusters. Here the upper bound of the 80% tail probability
ranks banks exactly as the implied volatility does, because both are
monotone in the same volatility:

```{r}
auc_test(lab, c("iv", "hi80"), ref = "iv", B = 200)
```

`auc_bounds()` gives the range of AUCs consistent with the quotes when each
score is only known to lie between its bounds:

```{r}
auc_bounds(lab$lo80, lab$hi80, lab$pos)
```

The range is wide: a point estimate of the tail probability may rank banks
well, but the quotes alone do not pin that ranking down.

`first_alarm()` returns the first date on which a score exceeds a threshold
for a run of consecutive observations.

```{r}
a <- lab[lab$bank == "A", ]
first_alarm(a$date, a$iv, threshold = 0.45, run = 2)
```

## References

Capuano, C. (2008). The option-iPoD: the probability of default implied by
option prices based on entropy. IMF Working Paper 08/194.

Dillschneider, Y. (2026). Option prices and option-implied probabilities in
incomplete markets. SSRN working paper 6976498.

Vilsmeier, J. (2016). Updating the option implied probability of default
methodology. Journal of Computational Finance 19(3), 1--27.
